name: Chess
intro: Learn chess from zero: how every piece moves, check and checkmate, the special moves, then the tactics and checkmate patterns that win games. Every lesson is hands-on, on a real board.

ladder.name: Penny
ladder.blurb: Just learned the moves. Leaves pieces hanging.

ladder.name: Mira
ladder.blurb: Solid club player. Punishes free pieces.

ladder.name: The Monocle
ladder.blurb: Calculates deep. Bring your best tactics.

units.name: How the pieces move
units.blurb: The board, the six pieces and how each one moves and captures.

lessons.title: The chess board and how to set it up
lessons.summary: How to set up a chess board: which way the board goes, where each of the 16 pieces starts, and who moves first.
lessons.wrap: That’s the starting position. Next, meet the pieces one at a time, starting with the rook.

steps.text:
Chess is played on a board of 64 squares, 8 by 8. Each player has 16 pieces: 8 pawns, 2 rooks, 2 knights, 2 bishops, a queen and a king.

White always moves first, then the players take turns.

Turn the board so each player has a light square in the bottom-right corner. A quick way to remember it: “light on the right”.

The rooks go in the corners, then the knights, then the bishops. The pawns fill the row in front.
The queen starts on a square of her own colour: the white queen on a light square, the black queen on a dark one.
steps.prompt: Tap the white queen.
steps.wrong: Not that one. Look in the middle of White’s back row, on a light square.
steps.done: Right, d1. The king stands beside her on e1.

steps.text: Black’s pieces mirror White’s: queen on d8, king on e8.
steps.prompt: Tap the black king.
steps.wrong: Look along Black’s back row, next to the black queen.
steps.done: Yes, e8. The two kings face each other on the e-file.

steps.text: Quick check before we start moving pieces.
steps.prompt: Who makes the first move in a game of chess?
steps.explain: White always moves first. Players usually swap colours between games.

lessons.title: How the rook moves in chess
lessons.summary: The rook moves in straight lines along rows and columns, as far as it likes. Learn how it moves, what blocks it and how it captures.
lessons.wrap: The rook is worth about 5 pawns. Next up: the bishop, which moves on the diagonals.

steps.text:
The rook moves in a straight line: up, down, left or right, as many squares as it likes.

It can’t move diagonally, and it can’t jump over other pieces.
On an empty board the rook on d4 can reach 14 squares.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the rook can move to.
steps.wrong: The rook can’t go there. It only moves along its row and its column.
steps.done: All 14. Notice the rook controls the same number of squares wherever it stands.

steps.text: Now there are other pieces in the way. The rook stops before its own pawn on d6, but it can capture the black knight on g4 by moving onto its square.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the rook can move to now.
steps.wrong: Blocked! The rook can’t jump over pieces, and it can’t land on its own pawn.
steps.done: Exactly. The knight’s square counts, but nothing behind it does.

steps.text: Your turn to move.
steps.prompt: Capture the black knight with the rook.
steps.wrong: That’s a legal move, but it doesn’t capture. Move the rook onto the knight’s square.
steps.done: Captured! The knight is removed from the board.

lessons.title: How the bishop moves in chess
lessons.summary: The bishop moves diagonally as far as it likes and always stays on squares of one colour. Learn how it moves and captures.
lessons.wrap: The bishop is worth about 3 pawns. Next: the queen, who moves like a rook and a bishop together.

steps.text:
The bishop moves diagonally, as far as it likes, and can’t jump over pieces.

Because it only moves diagonally, a bishop stays on one colour for the whole game. Each player has one light-squared and one dark-squared bishop.
From the centre a bishop reaches the most squares.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the bishop can move to.
steps.wrong: The bishop can’t go there. It only moves along diagonals.
steps.done: 13 squares, all of them light, like the bishop’s own square.

steps.text: Think about the colours of the squares.
steps.prompt: Can this bishop ever reach a dark square?
steps.explain: Never. Every diagonal step lands on the same colour, so a light-squared bishop stays on light squares all game.

steps.text: The black rook is on the bishop’s diagonal.
steps.prompt: Capture the rook with your bishop.
steps.wrong: Follow the diagonal from your bishop up to the right.
steps.done: A bishop for a rook would already be a good trade, but here you got the rook for free.

lessons.title: How the queen moves in chess
lessons.summary: The queen moves any distance in a straight line or diagonally. She is the most powerful piece, worth about 9 pawns.
lessons.wrap: The queen is your strongest piece, so don’t lose her cheaply. Next: the knight, the only piece that jumps.

steps.text:
The queen moves like a rook and a bishop: any distance along a row, a column or a diagonal.

She can’t jump over pieces, but from the middle of the board she controls 27 squares.
Three of the marked squares are in the queen’s reach.
steps.prompt: Tap the marked square the queen can’t reach in one move.
steps.wrong: The queen can reach that one. Look for a square that isn’t on a straight line or a diagonal from d4.
steps.done: Right. e6 isn’t on any of the queen’s lines.

steps.text: When a piece attacks the enemy king, that’s called check.
steps.prompt: Move the queen to attack the black king.
steps.done: Check! The king is attacked and Black must deal with it.

steps.text: Players use rough values to judge trades: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5.
steps.prompt: About how many pawns is a queen worth?
steps.explain: About 9. That’s why losing your queen for a smaller piece usually loses the game.

lessons.title: How the knight moves in chess
lessons.summary: The knight moves in an L shape and is the only chess piece that can jump over others. Practise its moves on a real board.
lessons.wrap: The knight is worth about 3 pawns, like a bishop. Next: the king.

steps.text:
The knight moves in an L shape: two squares in one direction, then one square to the side.

It’s the only piece that can jump over other pieces, and it always lands on the opposite colour.
From the centre a knight has 8 squares to choose from.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the knight can jump to.
steps.wrong: Not an L shape. Count two squares one way, then one to the side.
steps.done: All 8. They make a circle around the knight.

steps.text: Because it jumps, a knight can move at the very start of the game, over its own pawns.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the knight on g1 can jump to.
steps.wrong: The knight can’t land on its own pawn, and it must move in an L.
steps.done: f3 and h3. f3 is usually the better square: closer to the centre.

steps.text: Knights are sneaky because their attacks don’t follow straight lines.
steps.prompt: Capture the rook with your knight.
steps.wrong: That doesn’t capture. Find the L-shaped jump onto the rook.
steps.done: Got it. A knight for nothing: well, a rook for nothing.

lessons.title: How the king moves in chess
lessons.summary: The king moves one square in any direction and can never move into check. Learn the king’s moves and the one rule it must always follow.
lessons.wrap: Keep your king safe: if it’s trapped, you lose. Next: the pawns.

steps.text:
The king moves one square in any direction.

It’s the most important piece: if your king is trapped, you lose the game.
A king in the middle of an empty board has 8 squares.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the king can move to.
steps.wrong: The king only moves one square at a time.
steps.done: All 8 neighbours.

steps.text: The golden rule: a king can never move into check, onto a square an enemy piece attacks. Here the black rook controls the whole d-file.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the king can move to now.
steps.wrong: That square is attacked by the rook. The king can’t step into check.
steps.done: Right. The three squares on the d-file are off-limits.

steps.text: The two kings are two squares apart.
steps.prompt: Can the white king move to d4?
options: No, the kings would be next to each other
steps.explain: No. A king can never stand next to the other king, because it would be moving into check.

lessons.title: How pawns move and capture in chess
lessons.summary: Pawns move straight forward but capture diagonally, and can move two squares on their first move. Learn every pawn rule with practice.
lessons.wrap: Pawns are worth 1 each, but they decide a lot of games. Next: captures and what the pieces are worth.

steps.text:
A pawn moves straight forward one square. On its very first move it may go two squares instead.

Pawns never move backwards.
This pawn hasn’t moved yet.
steps.prompt: Tap every square the pawn can move to.
steps.wrong: Pawns only move straight forward.
steps.done: One or two squares: it’s the pawn’s first move.

steps.text: Here’s the twist: pawns capture diagonally, one square forward to either side. And a piece directly in front blocks a pawn.
steps.prompt: Tap every square this pawn can move to.
steps.wrong: The knight in front blocks the pawn. Pawns can’t capture straight ahead.
steps.done: Only the two diagonal captures. The pawn can’t go forward.

steps.text: Pawns are perfect for attacking bigger pieces.
steps.prompt: Capture the knight with your pawn.
steps.wrong: Capture diagonally, onto the knight’s square.
steps.done: A pawn worth 1 just took a knight worth 3.

lessons.title: Capturing and chess piece values
lessons.summary: How captures work in chess and what each piece is worth: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. Use the values to choose good trades.
lessons.wrap: You know how every piece moves. Next unit: check and checkmate, how the game is actually won.

steps.text:
You capture by moving onto an enemy piece’s square. The captured piece leaves the board for good.

To judge a capture, count points: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king can’t be captured: the game ends first.
Your knight on e5 attacks three black pieces.
steps.prompt: Make the most valuable capture.
steps.wrong: That works, but there’s a bigger prize. Which piece is worth the most?
steps.done: The queen, worth 9. Always check what your pieces attack.

steps.text: You can take a rook with your bishop, but then your opponent takes your bishop back.
steps.prompt: Is that a good trade for you?
steps.explain: Yes. You gain 5 points and give up 3, so you come out 2 ahead. Chess players call this “winning the exchange”.

units.name: Check and checkmate
units.blurb: How the game is won, and the draw you need to avoid.

lessons.title: Check in chess and the three ways out
lessons.summary: What check means in chess and the three ways to get out of it: move the king, block the attack, or capture the attacking piece.
lessons.wrap: Move, block or capture: remember those three. Next: checkmate.

steps.text:
When your king is attacked it is in check, and you must get out of check straight away.

There are only three ways: move the king, block the attack, or capture the attacker.
Way one: move the king to a safe square.
steps.prompt: Get your king out of check.
steps.done: Safe. Notice e2 wasn’t allowed: the rook still attacks it.

steps.text: Way two: block by putting a piece between the attacker and your king.
steps.prompt: Block the check with your bishop.
steps.wrong: That escapes too, but this time block: put the bishop between the rook and your king.
steps.done: Blocked. The rook can’t see through the bishop.

steps.text: Way three: capture the piece giving check. Often the best way of all.
steps.prompt: Capture the checking rook.
steps.wrong: That gets out of check, but you can do better: capture the rook.
steps.done: The threat is gone and you won a rook.

steps.text: One last rule.
steps.prompt: Can you ever make a move that leaves your own king in check?
steps.explain: Never. A move that leaves your king in check is illegal, and the board here won’t let you make one.

lessons.title: What is checkmate in chess?
lessons.summary: Checkmate is check with no way out, and it wins the game. Learn to recognise checkmate and deliver your first ones.
lessons.wrap: That’s how chess games are won. Next: stalemate, the draw that catches beginners out.

steps.text:
Checkmate means the king is in check and there is no way out: it can’t move, the check can’t be blocked and the attacker can’t be captured.

Watch: the rook checks along the back row, and Black’s own pawns trap the king. Checkmate, White wins.
Here the rook could go to d8 too, but one of Black’s pawns has moved.
steps.prompt: Would Rd8 be checkmate here?
options: No, the king could escape to f7
steps.explain: No. With the f-pawn gone the king has an escape square on f7. Check, but not mate.

steps.text: Your turn. Your king guards the squares around the black king, and your queen can finish the job.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Checkmate! The king is attacked and every escape square is covered.

steps.text: A rook can do it too, with help from the king.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Mate. Your king covers f7, g7 and h7; the rook covers the whole back row.

lessons.title: What is stalemate in chess?
lessons.summary: Stalemate is when the player to move has no legal move but isn’t in check. It’s a draw. Learn to spot it and avoid throwing away a win.
lessons.wrap: Always check your opponent has a move left. Next unit: the special moves.

steps.text:
It’s Black’s turn. The black king isn’t in check, but every square it could go to is attacked, and Black has no other pieces.

That’s stalemate: the player to move has no legal move and is not in check. The game is a draw.
White has a whole queen more.
steps.prompt: Who wins this game?
steps.explain: Nobody. Stalemate is a draw however many pieces you have, so it’s the classic way to throw away a win.

steps.text: Careful here: some queen moves leave Black with no move at all.
steps.prompt: Checkmate, without stalemating.
steps.done: Mate, not stalemate. The king is in check, so it counts as a win.

units.name: Special moves
units.blurb: Castling, en passant and promotion: the three rules everyone forgets.

lessons.title: How to castle in chess
lessons.summary: Castling moves your king to safety and brings a rook into play in one move. Learn how to castle on both sides and when you’re not allowed to.
lessons.wrap: Castle early in most games. Next: en passant.

steps.text:
Castling is the only move where two pieces move at once. The king moves two squares towards a rook, and that rook jumps over to the square beside it.

It tucks your king away and brings the rook towards the centre.
To castle, move the king two squares. The rook follows by itself.
steps.prompt: Castle on the king’s side: move the king two squares to the right.
steps.wrong: Move the king itself two squares towards the h1 rook.
steps.done: Castled kingside. King on g1, rook on f1.

steps.text: You can also castle on the queen’s side, the long way.
steps.prompt: Castle queenside: move the king two squares to the left.
steps.wrong: Move the king two squares towards the a1 rook.
steps.done: Castled queenside. King on c1, rook on d1.

steps.text: Castling has conditions: the king and that rook must not have moved, the squares between them must be empty, and the king can’t be in check, pass through check or land in check.
steps.prompt: Your king is in check. Can you castle to escape?
steps.explain: No. You can’t castle out of check. Move, block or capture instead.

lessons.title: En passant: the chess rule explained
lessons.summary: En passant lets a pawn capture an enemy pawn that has just moved two squares past it. Learn the rule and practise it on a real board.
lessons.wrap: En passant only works on the very next move. Last special move: promotion.

steps.text:
Your pawn is on e5. Watch Black move a pawn two squares, landing right beside yours.

If it had moved one square, you could have captured it. So the rules let you capture it as if it had moved only one. That’s en passant, French for “in passing”.
Your pawn moves diagonally to the square the black pawn skipped over, and the black pawn is removed.
steps.prompt: Capture en passant.
steps.wrong: Move your pawn diagonally onto d6, behind the black pawn.
steps.done: En passant! The black pawn on d5 is gone.

steps.text: Timing matters.
steps.prompt: When can you capture en passant?
options: Any time later in the game
Only on the very next move
steps.explain: Only straight away. If you make another move first, the chance is gone.

lessons.title: Pawn promotion in chess
lessons.summary: A pawn that reaches the far side of the board is promoted to a queen, rook, bishop or knight. Learn the rule and promote your first pawn.
lessons.wrap: You know every rule of chess. Test yourself in the rules check.

steps.text:
When a pawn reaches the far side of the board, it promotes: you swap it for a queen, rook, bishop or knight of your colour.

Almost everyone picks a queen. You can have two or more queens at once.
Here the lesson board promotes to a queen for you.
steps.prompt: Push your pawn and promote it.
steps.done: A new queen, and she even gives check.

steps.text: One more question.
steps.prompt: Which piece can a pawn not promote to?
steps.explain: A king. You only ever have one king.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Prove you know the rules, then move on to strategy.

lessons.title: Chess rules quiz
lessons.summary: Test your knowledge of the chess rules: piece moves, check, checkmate, stalemate, castling, en passant and promotion.
lessons.wrap: You’ve passed the rules check. Now the fun part: tactics that win games.

steps.text: Question 1.
steps.prompt: Which marked square can the knight jump to?
steps.wrong: Not an L shape from d4.
steps.done: Right: two up, one across.

steps.text: Question 2.
steps.prompt: Which is true about castling?
options: You can castle after moving your king, if it’s back home
steps.explain: The king moves two squares and the rook hops over it. Once the king has moved, castling is gone for good.

steps.text: Question 3.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Mate on the back row.

steps.text: Question 4. It’s Black’s turn.
steps.prompt: What’s the result?
steps.explain: Stalemate. Black isn’t in check but has no legal move, so it’s a draw.

steps.text: Question 5.
steps.prompt: A pawn moves two squares and lands beside your pawn. When can you capture it en passant?
options: Only on your very next move
steps.explain: Only on the very next move.

steps.text: Question 6. The black bishop is checking your king.
steps.prompt: Get out of check.
steps.done: Out of check. Moving the king or blocking on c3 or d2 all work.

units.name: Winning material
units.blurb: Forks, pins, skewers and free pieces: the tactics that decide most games.

lessons.title: Spotting free pieces in chess
lessons.summary: Most beginner games are won by grabbing pieces that aren’t protected. Learn to check what is defended before you capture.
lessons.wrap: Before every move ask: what does my opponent attack, and what can I take for free?

steps.text:
A piece is hanging (or “free”) when you can capture it and nothing can capture back.

Here White can take two pieces, but only one of them is free.
The knight on f6 is protected by the pawn on g7. The bishop on b4 isn’t protected by anything.
steps.prompt: Take the free piece.
steps.wrong: That piece is defended: you’d lose your piece back. Look for the unprotected one.
steps.done: Free bishop. Nothing can take your queen back.

steps.text: Good players run the same check before every move.
steps.prompt: Which question catches the most mistakes?
options: Which piece have I moved least?
steps.explain: Always look at your opponent’s last move and ask what it threatens. It stops you leaving pieces hanging.

lessons.title: The knight fork in chess
lessons.summary: A fork attacks two pieces at once. Learn the knight fork, one of the most common chess tactics, with puzzles on a real board.
lessons.wrap: Look out for squares where your knight attacks the king and another piece at once.

steps.text:
A fork is one piece attacking two at the same time. Your opponent can only save one.

Knights are the best forkers: here the knight checks the king and attacks the rook. The king must move, and then the rook falls.
Find the fork, then collect the prize.
steps.prompt: Fork the king and rook.
steps.good: Check and fork! Black moves the king…
steps.done: Rook won.

steps.text: This one wins the queen.
steps.prompt: Find the knight fork.
steps.good: Check, and the queen is attacked too. Black’s king steps away…
steps.done: Queen won with a single knight.

lessons.title: Pins and skewers in chess
lessons.summary: A pin stops a piece moving because something more valuable is behind it. A skewer is the reverse. Learn both with puzzles.
lessons.wrap: Pins and skewers come from bishops, rooks and queens on long lines. Next: checkmate patterns.

steps.text: A pin: the bishop attacks the knight, and behind the knight is the king. The knight can’t move, because that would expose the king to check.
A pinned piece is a sitting duck. Attack it again!
steps.prompt: Attack the pinned knight with a pawn.
steps.wrong: Use the pawn to attack the knight. It can’t run away.
steps.done: The knight is stuck and will be lost.

steps.text: A skewer is a pin in reverse: you attack the more valuable piece first. When it moves, you take the piece behind it.
The king and queen are on the same row.
steps.prompt: Skewer the king and queen.
steps.good: Check along the row. The king has to move…
steps.done: Skewered! The queen is yours.

units.name: Checkmate patterns
units.blurb: The mates that come up again and again, and how to finish a won game.

lessons.title: The back rank mate in chess
lessons.summary: The back rank mate traps a king behind its own pawns. Learn to deliver it and to protect your own king from it.
lessons.wrap: Watch for kings stuck behind their own pawns, and give your own king some air.

steps.text: A king that has castled often sits behind three pawns. That’s safe, until a rook or queen reaches the back rank. The pawns become a cage.
Black’s king has no escape square.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Back rank mate!

steps.text: The queen can do it too.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Mate. The pawns on f7, g7 and h7 trap their own king.

steps.text: Black has pushed the h-pawn one square.
steps.prompt: Would Rd8+ still be mate?
options: No, the king escapes to h7
steps.explain: No. That little pawn move gave the king a window on h7. Making one is the easiest way to stop back rank mates.

lessons.title: How to checkmate with a queen and king
lessons.summary: Practise the queen and king checkmate: push the enemy king to the edge, bring your king close, and avoid stalemate.
lessons.wrap: With a queen up, push the king to the edge, bring your own king close, and check for stalemate before every move.

steps.text:
A queen and king can always force checkmate. The method: the queen pushes the enemy king to the edge, then your king comes close to help.

Here the job is almost done.
Your king covers g7 and h7.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Mate along the back row.

steps.text: The king is in the corner and your king guards a7, b7 and b8… almost.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Mate.

steps.text: Careful: several queen moves here are stalemate.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move, without stalemating.
steps.done: Mate, not stalemate. Well spotted.

lessons.title: The ladder mate with two rooks
lessons.summary: Two rooks can checkmate a lone king without help, taking turns to push it to the edge. Learn the ladder mate step by step.
lessons.wrap: Two rooks climb the ladder in turns. The same idea works with a queen and a rook.

steps.text:
The ladder mate: one rook guards a row, the other gives check on the next row up. The king is pushed back one row at a time until it reaches the edge.

Here the rook on h5 already guards the 5th row.
Climb the ladder: check on the 6th row, then the 7th, then the 8th.
steps.prompt: Give check on the 6th row.
steps.next: Now the other rook climbs and checks.
steps.done: Checkmate! Down the ladder in three moves.

units.name: Opening principles
units.blurb: How to start a game well, and the trap every beginner falls into.

lessons.title: Chess opening principles for beginners
lessons.summary: The three opening principles every beginner should know: control the centre, develop your knights and bishops, and castle early.
lessons.wrap: Centre, develop, castle. Follow those and you’ll get a good game every time.

steps.text:
You don’t need to memorise openings. Follow three principles:

1. Control the centre (the four marked squares). 2. Develop your knights and bishops. 3. Castle to keep your king safe.
The best first moves grab the centre with a pawn and open lines for your pieces.
steps.prompt: Push a centre pawn two squares.
steps.wrong: That’s legal, but push one of the two middle pawns (d or e) two squares.
steps.done: The most popular first moves in chess.

steps.text: Black replied in the centre too. Now bring out a piece.
steps.prompt: Develop a knight or bishop towards the centre.
steps.wrong: Bring out a knight or bishop towards the centre. Avoid moving the queen early.
steps.done: Developed. Nf3 even attacks Black’s e5 pawn.

steps.text: One of these is a common beginner mistake.
steps.prompt: Which is the weakest plan in the opening?
options: Bring the queen out early to grab pawns
steps.explain: Moving the queen early lets your opponent attack her while developing their pieces, gaining time.

lessons.title: Scholar’s mate and how to stop it
lessons.summary: Scholar’s mate is the four-move checkmate that catches beginners. Learn how it works and the simple move that stops it.
lessons.wrap: Now you know the trap from both sides. Time to test yourself against the practice bots.

steps.text:
Watch the opening. White aims the bishop and queen at f7, the weakest square in Black’s camp: only the king protects it.

Black’s last move attacks the queen, but misses the threat.
The queen and bishop both hit f7.
steps.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
steps.done: Scholar’s mate! Checkmate in four moves.

steps.text: Now you’re Black, after White’s queen comes to h5.
steps.prompt: What’s the best defence?
steps.explain: …g6 blocks the queen’s path and kicks her next move. …Nf6 attacks the queen but allows Qxf7 mate. (…Qe7 also works.)
